name: Dining Philosophers
miniText: How can independent processes share exclusive resources without becoming permanently blocked? NetLogo Dining Philosophers places agents and forks around a ring; agents alternate between thinking, hunger, and eating, requiring both adjacent forks to eat. Dijkstra [1] supplies the classic synchronization context, Coffman and colleagues [2] analyze deadlock, and Chandy and Misra [3] develop related distributed resource coordination. The NetLogo switch compares a naive acquisition rule with a cooperative marking protocol, starting from one distinguished fork. One randomly selected philosopher updates per tick, making scheduling part of the baseline. The experiment illustrates how local ownership rules can alter global progress and fairness. A run without deadlock is not a proof of starvation freedom, and symmetric initial conditions or a different scheduler may change behavior. The cooperative teaching rule should not be identified automatically with every published solution.
